content: An iodate is a chemical compound that is classified as a salt derived from iodic acid. In the iodate anion (IO3−), the iodine atom is covalently bonded to three oxygen atoms, forming a structure with a trigonal pyramidal molecular geometry. Iodates can be synthesized by reducing periodate ions using a thioether as the reducing agent. This chemical reaction produces a sulfoxide as a byproduct. Iodates are a group of compounds that contain the iodate anion. Examples of such compounds include sodium iodate (NaIO3), silver iodate (AgIO3), and calcium iodate (Ca(IO3)2). Structurally, iodates are similar to chlorates, except that the central atom is iodine instead of chlorine. Under acidic conditions, iodates can react to form iodic acid. Potassium hydrogen iodate (KH(IO3)2) is an example of a double salt that contains both potassium iodate and iodic acid, and it also exhibits acidic properties. Iodates are commonly utilized in chemical experiments, such as the iodine clock reaction, which is a well-known demonstration of chemical kinetics.
